mittee. The instructions were in the first place to post up these proposed delimitations in every county and city throughout the united kingdom in order that any elector from one end of the country to the other might go before the delimitation committee find state liis objections to tlie proposed delimitation. There was no word then from one end of the country to the other in opposition to the conference, and there could not he a possible objection to the delimitation. What was the ease in the committee of which I had the honour of being a member to which the whole question now before the House was referred ? I accepted the committee, as I stated before, because I believed it to be a conference between the different parties, and that any question as to the delimitation of a country or a riding that we could not agree upon ourselves would not be resolved by the simple majority of the committee, but, that there would be some way found for settling^ the difficulty and that any way the committee should be guided by a set of principles in in delimiting the constituencies. The first question that came up was as to whether the cities of Montreal and Toronto were to receive equal representation with other port-tions of the country according to population. The representation of the city of Montreal and the whole province of Quebec was agreed upon unanimously with the concurrence of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) without the application of any principle at all. Almost the same thing took place in regard to New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward Island and almost the same in reference to British Columbia the North-west Territories and Manitoba. There were slight differences of opinion only, but when it came to the lighting ground between the two parties in this country-the province of Ontario- there was no principle to guide the committee. The hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) stated that there were simply three propositions put before the committee and that these were all that were voted upon. X know of twenty myself. I remember them. If necessary I will read them out. The first proposition that was made before the committee was one for the adoption of a principle to guide the committee as to the delimitation of constituencies. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition moved :
la accordance with the principle laid down by the Prime Minister in the House on the introduction of the Bill, municipal boundaries shall be observed.
We moved that as a principle. It was voted down. Then again :
Where separate representation Is given to cities, the municipal boundaries of such cities shall be observed.
Not voted down but refused :
3. (a.) The municipal county boundaries shall be those set forth in chapter 3, Revised Statutes

of Ontario, 1807, and that the word ' county ' herein shall Include any provisional county or territorial district established by ithe said Act.
(b.) The separate representation to be allotted to cities of Ontario shall be first fixed and determined before proceeding with the representation of the rural constituencies.
(c.) The unit of representation for such rural constituencies shall be determined by deducting from the total population of Ontario the combined population of the said cities and by dividing the remainder by the total number of seats to be allotted to rural constituencies.
(d.) The population of any city receiving separate representation shall be excluded in computing the population of the county within which it is situate.
(e.) The redistribution of ithe representation pf Ontario shall then be determined 'as follows
We wanted to he guided by fixed principles in the delimitation which the committee had to make in Ontario. We moved this resolution. Is there a single member on the other side of the House or does the bon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) object to a single principle embodied in that resolution ?
I do and I will give the hon. gentleman my reasons in a moment.
Very likely we shall have the reasons. Is there any objection to the one that municipal county boundaries shall be observed ?
There was no objection to that.

Is there an objection to the one which says :
Where separate representation is given to cities the municipal representation of such cities shall be observed.
Or to the clause which says:
The municipal county boundaries shall be those set forth in chapter 3 of the Revised Statutes of Ontario.
Which was agreed to by the hon. Minister of Justice.
There is no objection to that.

Is there any objection to the clause providing :
The separate representation to be allotted to cities of Ontario shall be first fixed and determined before proceeding with the representation of the rural constituencies.
That was agreed to.

Then there is the clause :
The unit of representation for such rural and civic constituencies shall be determined by deducting from the total population, &c.
I do not suppose the hon. minister objects to that.
The population of any city receiving separate representation shall be excluded in computing the population of the county within which it is situated.

I have got now to the clause to which the hon. gentleman objects. I did not notice it before. That clause would prevent him from getting that extra member for Middlesex.
It was put there for that purpose.

Then we have the clause :
The redistribution of Ontario shali then be determined as follows :-
The only clause to which he can possibly have objection is that providing that in awarding the number of representatives to the different constituencies the population of cities shall be deducted from the population of the counties in which they are situated. We proposed a set of principles for the delimitation of the different constituencies. If there was anything wrong in the principles we proposed, why did the hon. gentleman not propose another set of principles for the purpose of guiding the committee ? The hon. Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) said at the time: Oh, I think the principles are perfectly right but we do not want to be bound down by strict, iron-clad rules, we want a little latitude in the delimitation of the different constituencies. What has been the result of that latitude ? I do not think that the Minister of Public Works (Plon. Mr. Sutherland) or any member of the committee will deny that political considerations entered into the delimitation. If that was not the case why was the county of Leeds divided as it was ? Why did you divide Hastings as you proposed to do, although it was changed the other day ? Why did you make such an extraordinary delimitation of the county of Waterloo, unless it was for political purposes ? Why is it that the county of Grey is delimited in its present form ? Then look at the county of Kent, an old county whose form had not been changed since its original construction. From the beginning the townships were bordered by the river which is a natural dividing line between the townships from one end of the county to the other and there could not be a more fair or equitable division, according to population, community or of interest or any other principle than that which previously existed. The county of Brant also would have been delimited in a different manner if hon. gentlemen had adhered to the principles adopted by Mr. Gladstone, Lord Salisbury and those who sat in the conference in England. According to these principles rural population would not have been added to the city of Brantford although that population is less than the number which would entitle it to a representative. Owing to the principle of community of interest the urban population would be separated from the rural population and in this case there is the strongest reason for such a division because, if my information is correct, the population of Brantford, according to the municipal
census, is now in the neighbourhood of 20,000. In all these counties a delimitation was made not according to any principle but according to the political exigencies of the party. It was not made as the result of any evidence brought before the committee, there was no evidence in reference to Waterloo or Brantford. Waterloo had been divided in the same manner for Dominion and local purposes and its representation had nearly always been the same.
The MINISTER OF PL'BLIC WORKS. Was not the reason given for making the change in Waterloo the desire to avoid dividing the townships? I do not think my hon. friend would advocate the principle of dividing townships or small municipalities.

I do not remember any reason of the kind being advanced but if it is dividing the townships they have been divided by the Dominion Act from time immemorial and they are to-day divided both for the Dominion and the local.

The dividing of townships was condemned in this House, especially by the Conservative party, and the county of Waterloo was particularly criticised. It was to avoid doing that and only that, that we made the change.

That was particularly to be avoided. When did the Minister of Public Works get new light which led him to change his mind and the decision of the committee in reference to it and put it back In its old form ?

It was not to establish a precedent. The constituency has been divided in that way for Dominion and provincial purposes for a long time, as the hon. gentleman has said, and by agreement a rule which I do not think any person in this House would advocate has been allowed to apply to two townships in the whole Dominion.
The Minister of Public Works may be perfectly right.
If my hon. friend will look at the record he will see that that is the reason which I gave at the time.

It may have been the reason that influenced him at the time but I do -not remember it and I suppose that I should have remembered if it had been so. The division made by the Minister of Public Works and the majority of the committee in reference to Waterloo was so distasteful even to his own party that they have changed it in the Bill and restored the constituency to the original form.

I would like the hon. gentleman to give any evidence that this was distasteful to any Liberal in the House or in Waterloo county. I have never had any representation from-

any Liberal in the House or in Waterloo county that it was distasteful to them. If my hon. friend will look at the records he will see that we went further and said that a great many representations had been made to the committee to divide municipalities, and that I did not know how we could do it in one case and not in another.
In any case the House changed the delimitation of the county back to its original form.

The five counties with which the hon. member for South Norfolk proposed to deal with have a population of 139,338 with five members, or an average of

27.867	per member, whereas the three western counties, as I have said, have an average of 28,763 per member. When you come to deal with the matter of principle, if you have an extra member to give away, should not that extra member be assigned to three counties with an average of 28,763 rather than to five counties with an average of
27.867	? What principle is there in that ? There is no bon. gentleman who can point out any possible principle that is applicable to an amendment such as that.
Now, we seem to be fortunate in this redistribution in having before the House, not only the Bill itself, but also some proposed amendments. I understand, speaking from memory, that tlfe amendments proposed by the opposition number twenty-two, but when it comes to putting these amendments on record, how many of these amendments have been made in the House ? The plan of attack is a general one. The plan of attack is to use a large number of exaggerated adjectives, but when it comes to a discussion of the details of the meas'ure, there has not been very much said about them in the House. We have only on record so far, in reference to the province of Ontario, five amendments, net us see what they are. The bon. member for South Norfolk has put on record the amendment which I have just read with regard to the five counties in the Niagara peninsula, which, I think, Mr. Speaker, I have shown does not involve any matter of principle. Mr. Monk moved a resolution re the townships of Clara, Maria and Head. Notwithstanding the fact that the arrangement was accepted by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) and by the hon. member for South Lanark {Hon. Mr. Haggart), there is a motion before the House to change these three municipalities back from Nipissiug to Renfrew. Then there was also a motion re Leeds. Mr. Yrooman introduced a motion re Victoria, Mr. Richardson re Grey and air. Clancy re Kent. I think this is the total number of resolutions before the House. I have nothing more to say, except that in the discussion from the other side of the House it was argued over and over again that you had to take the results of the election to prove that the redistribution of 1882 was not entered into for the purpose of striking a blow at the Liberal party.
It is quite true that after the elections of 1882, a largely increased number of members of the Liberal party were returned to this House. It is well known that this was due to that very redistribution, because there were so many Conservatives throughout the whole of Ontario, who felt that an unfair advantage was being taken, and who, for that reason, left their political party
and voted with the Liberals. Therefore, I quite agree that the Conservative party did not get the full fruits of their work in the next election. In the present instance lion, gentlemen opposite, in seeking to make an argument against the present redistribution, take the vote at the last election, apply it to the present redistribution, and say that the Liberal party is going to make so many gains by this redistribution. The whole matter, to my mind, is a matter for the electors of Ontario to decide upon ; if they can be persuaded that the Liberal party have deliberately gerrymandered the constituencies of Ontario for party gain, exactly the same result will accrue to the Liberal party as accrued to the Conservative party in 18S2, so that the hon. gentlemen can have nothing to complain of. But if we restored what was taken away from us, if the redistribution on the face of it is a fair and just redistribution, taking into consideration all the circumstances and difficulties the committee had to meet, then it may be quite true that in the case of the counties which had been interfered with, and which of necessity have now gone back into their original shape by reason of adhering to the principle of county boundaries, it may be quite true that certain gains will come to the Liberal party. Surely there can be no objection to that; it is a matter for the country to pass judgment upon, and so far as I am concerned, speaking as a member of the committee, I am perfectly satisfied that the country should judge.

I went to that gentleman myself, and asked him if it was a correct statement. I told him I had gone over the figures myself, and could not verify it or bring out any such result. Mr. Speaker, a few evenings ago I attempted to say something on this gerrymander, but it seems that I was out of order, and therefore I was unable to do so. Therefore I avail myself of the present opportunity. The hon. gentleman who has preceded me argued that this was a fair redistribution measure. Now, I happen to be one of the members of the House whose seats are wiped out by this Bill. I listened with delight to the speech of the right hon. the Prime Minister in introducing it, in which he laid down the principles on which the redistribution was to take place. I inferred from his remarks that there was a very good chance of the county of Cardwell continuing to be a constituency. He stated that he was going to right the wrongs that had been done by the gerrymander of 1882. Well knowing that there had been no gerrymander of the county I represented, and that there was no wrong to be righted in that case, I thought it would surely escape being gerrymandered out of existence by this Bill. I find that the county of Cardwell was formed in the year 1867, at the time of confederation and that it has been a constituency undisturbed from that day to this. It is a constituency with a history, and that history if nothing else should have been sufficient reason for not wiping out of existence a constituency which had been represented by so many prominent men in the past. The first man who represented Cardwell in this House was the late Hon. Thomas Ferguson ; the next was the late Hon. John Hil-yard Cameron ; the next was the late Dalton McCarthy ; the next was the. late Hon. Thomas White, Minister of the Interior ; the next was Mr. It. S. White ; the next was Mr. William Stubbs ; and now your humble servant is endeavouring to represent it as best he knows how. During the last three sessions, in which I have been trying to represent that .constituency, I have endeavoured to be as agreeable as possible to all the members of this House, and to avoid saying anything offensive to any one. The right hon. leader of the government said that in this Bill he would try to maintain old landmarks. Well, If the constituency of Cardwell is not an old landmark, I do not know what constituency in the Dominion of Canada is; because ever since confederation it has been a constituency undisturbed. From the promises made by bon. gentlemen opposite of what they would do for the farmers of this country if they secured power, we naturally expected great things from them. But in looking over the list of representatives of the constituency of Cardwell, I find that I have the honour of being the only farmer who ever represented that constituency in this House ; and the first time that old historic constituency is represented by a farmer, it is wiped out of existence by this Liberal government who promised to give the far-

mers fair-play, and to do so much for them. I notice that other constituencies represented by farmers as well as the constituency of Cardwell have come to grief in this redistribution. Out of the constituencies which have been lost to the province of Ontario, I find that seven are represented by farmers and one by a professional man. That is one thing that lion, gentlemen opposite have done most completely by this gerrymander Act-they have wiped out the farmers politically wherever they could get a chance to do it. If lam not mistaken, the feeling of the people throughout the Dominion of Canada is that there should be more farmers here and fewer professional men. Although the farmers may not have as much ability to explain their views on the floor of this House, I think the people of Canada have as much faith in their honesty and their ability to represent them, as they have in professional men. But, this government, for the first time in the Dominion of Canada, has evidently made a specialty of wiping out the farmers' constituencies, because no other gerrymander that has been adopted in this country has wiped out so many farmers' seats in the province of Ontario. Strange to say, too, although this is a favourable gerrymander from the standpoint of the government, it happens that in the whole batch of those who have lost their constituencies, there is only one Reform farmer, the hon. member for South Middlesex (Mr. McGugan). I suppose that if this government remains in power long enough, it will see that that farmer gets a better job than that of a representative here. I do not think my chances are quite as good in that respect as his. However, on account of his being a farmer, I shall have no grievance if they do give him a pretty good job.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that only one Liberal seat is wiped out ?
Only one farmer's seat.
You are not a farmer.
I do not pretend to be a farmer, as the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) sometimes does.

I am glad you are not. If you were it would certainly be another slur on the farmers. Although this county has never been gerrymandered from a Dominion standpoint, it has been by the Ontario government, anl several times we have awakened and hardly known where we were. The township of Caledon, in which I am living, was first in the county of Peel and then put into Cardwell, and two townships were taken off Peel and added to Cardwell. We would wake up one
morning and find ourselves in the county of Cardwell and then wake up another morning and find ourselves back in the county of Peel. Two townships had been taken out of the county of Peel by the Ontario gerrymander. They then put back Caledon into the county of Peel and left the township of Albion in the county of Cardwell. Although there has been very little change in the county of Cardwell, in fact, no change from the Dominion standpoint, there have been many from the Ontario standpoint. By the Ontario gerrymander it was made something like 100 miles long, and at one particular place it was only three miles wide. Yet we are told that this government is anxious to do only what is just and right. That will not be the judgment of the farmers of Ontario, whom the government seem to think that they can treat just as they please, and who seem to have very little influence with this government, although they are larger in number than all the other classes combined. I suppose it would not matter, even if I were to speak for six weeks, the government would not restore the county of Cardwell to its former position. Several times I have heard the right hon. gentleman say that if there could be justification shown him for leaving a county as it was, he would not change it. Well, if he will second a motion of mine, I think we can arrange so that there will not be nearly so much grievance for the farming community as his gerrymander will give rise to. But if he will not second my motion, there is no use of my getting a seconder on this side, for that will only take up time, and we will be calling for a vote to no effect. A great deal has been said about the iniquitous gerrymander of 1882 during this debate, and hon. gentlemen opposite have referred to their gerrymander as not being any worse. But if it be not better, they should condemn it as they did the redistribution of 1882. Take the great city of Toronto, which has been so much talked about, and which is so well represented in this House. If the right lion, gentleman would agree to second my motion, I world gladly move to leave Toronto and the Yorks as they are and not change the boundaries of Cardwell. If they will not do that on my account, let them do it for the sake of those who represented that old county in its early days.

Amendment (Hon. Mr. Haggart) negatived.

I desire to move the following amendment, seconded by Mr. Lefurgey :
That clause one be amended by erasing * four ' in the fifth line and substituting ' six ' therefor.
(la.) The county of King's shall form an electoral district to be called the electoral district of King's and shall return two members.
Ob.) The county of Prince shall form an electoral district to be called the electoral district of Prince and shall return two members.
(ic.) The counity of Queen's shall form an electoral district to be called the electoral district of Queen's and shall return two members.

I submit that this amendment is out of order, because it is contrary to the constitution. The constitution provides for representation by population between the provinces. The very question raised in this amendment has been submitted to the Supreme Court, which has decided that the province of Prince Edward Island and all the other provinces are entitled to the number of members which are mentioned in this Bill. The British North America Act provides that the representation of the other provinces shall be based upon the unit fixed by the representation of Quebec, and this amendment would violate that provision of the British North America Act.

I beg to say that I am not the seconder of that motion, the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) is the seconder of the motion before the Chair. As to the point of order raised, I understood that when my hon. friend (Mr. Hackett) brought this question up some time ago in the House, he was shut off, and was told that he could move this motion on the third reading and then take the sense of the House upon it.

The point of order has been raised that according to the constitution of the Dominion, Prince Edward Island is entitled to only four members. This motion provides for giving it six members. Therefore I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hackett) had better withdraw his motion.

This question lias not been definitely decided by the court, as an appeal is to be taken by the Prince Edward Island legislature to the Privy Council of Great Britain. I do not understand that tliis parliament is to be bound by the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada on this question. Therefore it seems to me this question may be legitimately discussed by this parliament at the present time.
Does the hon. gentleman want to press his motion or to withdraw it ?

I am speaking to the point of order. This question was brought up in the House and fully discussed by me earlier in the session, and while I do not intend on this occasion to make any lengthy remarks, I feel that the position of the island makes it the duty of the Prince Edward Island members to stand up and endeavour to get a fair representation for the province in this parliament.
I am afraid the hon. gentleman is not speaking to the point of order.
Order. I would invite the hon. gentleman to coniine his remarks to the point of order which has been raised.

I submit that the decision of the Supreme Court on this question does not bind this parliament. The Chief Justice expressely stated :
Of course this is not a usual case. We do not give a judgment, nothing but an opinion. It binds nobody.
I think, therefore, seeing that this was only an expression of opinion of the Supreme Court, that we have a right to get the judgment of this House upon the question as to whether Prince Edward Island is entitled to six members. I think that is a fair matter for discussion. With your permission I will go on with my remarks.

A point of order has been raised, and before the hon. gentleman can proceed with his remarks we have to dispose of the point of order. If the motion is not in order, then it would be useless for the hon. gentleman to proceed with his remarks.

Might I submit that since the decision of the Supreme Court was not a judgment of the court but merely an expression of opinion, it can in no way bind this parliament. Now if it is not a judgment of the court, I submit that the province can appeal against the decision. An expression of opinion of the Supreme Court can in no way change or alter the British North America Act.

The point is this : My hon. friend knows that the British North America Act says that after each census there shall be a redistribution according to population, the unit of representation being the representation of Quebec. My hon. friend knows that the census has been taken, and according to that census Prince Edward Island is entitled to only four members.
I always understood there was a special provision for Prince Edward Island ?

The people of Prince Edward claim that under that special provision in the Act they are entitled to have no decrease in their representation. I have only to observe on that point that they have already, under two former redistributions, lost two members. They had six, and they were reduced to four. When that reduction took place there was no protest on the part of Prince Edward Island. Now this Act of 1903 has been referred to the Supreme Court. The court did not give any judgment upon that, it only expressed an opinion for the guidance of parliament. My hon. friend raises a doubt as to the force of that decision. Here we are proceeding strictly according to the rules of parliament. My hon. friend says there is an exception in favour of Prince Edward Island, but that exception has already been broken on two previous occasions. The last argument my hon. friend makes is that there is to be an appeal to the Privy Council. There is no appeal, so far, to the Privy Council, and there can be no appeal as a matter of right. There cau be an appeal as a matter of grace, if the members of the law, members of the Privy Council see fit to grant it. Now the hon. gentleman is asking us that Prince Edward Island be given two more members than parliament has power to give them, because this is not a matter in which parliament has any discretion, it is settled by the terms of the British North America Act.
The Supreme Court's opinion decides nothing.

The Act provides that there shall be a representation on the floor of this House according to population, so far there is no question. According to that provision of the British North America Act, Prince Edward Island is entitled to four members. They claim an exception in their favour, but the Supreme Court has given an opinion that the exception claimed in their favour does not exist.
The only thing against the island is that it has submitted to a reduction after the last decennial census.

As it is now nearly six o'clock, and I have some doubts as to the point of order that has been raised, I will declare it six o'clock.
At six o'clock, House took recess.

After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

When we rose at six o'clock, the point of order had been raised as to whether a motion made by the hon. member for West Prince, P.E.I. (Mr. Hackett) was In order. The question which has been raised in regard to the amendment is a very important and it seems to me a very difficult one, and I am very sorry that I have not had more time at my disposal to give it the fullest consideration. It would appear, as has been stated before the House, that this parliament has not the necessary legislative authority to grant Prince Edward Island the number of members asked for by this amendment, and the Supreme Court, having been consulted upon the matter, declared that the British North America Act does not give to the province the right to have more than four members. The motion which was made would then be contrary to the law of the land, and to the constitution. According to rule 37 of the House of Commons, the Speaker has the right to declare out of order any motion contrary to the rules and privileges of parliament. I see that there is a very serious doubt, whether under our rules of procedure the Speaker has the right on his own authority to interfere and declare irregular and out of order a motion of this kind. May, at page 331, says :
But doubtful oases may arise, upon which the rules of the House are indistinct or obsolete, or do not apply strictly to the point at issue ; when the Speaker, being left without specific directions, refers the matter to the judgment of the house.
I am of the opinion, under the circumstances, that, on account of the serious doubt which may arise as. to the irregularity of the motion made by the hon. member for West Prince, I should leave it to the House to determine whether this motion is irregular or not, or whether it should be accepted or not.

Mr. Speaker, my amendment sets forth the fact that Prince Edward Island is entitled to a representation of six members in this House. I would like to have the parliament of Canada declare to-day whether or not our people are entitled to six members. I have already stated my views in regard to this, and I trust that' parliament will see its way clear to allow the people of Prince Edward Island six members instead of four.
The question is on the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I fail to understand how it is possible for this House to deal with this matter at the present time. The hon. member for West Prince, P.E.I. (Mr. Hackett) is aware that toy the constitution is was provided that Prince Edward Island came into

the confederation with the express stipulation that while six members were granted to it at the time it first came in, the representation of the province is to be readjusted from time to time under the provisions of the British North America Act. Readjustment must surely mean, that, in respect of Prince Edward Island, the provisions of the British North America Act wThich are applicable to all the other provinces must l>e equally applicable to that province. Readjustment must mean that each time the census is taken the representation of the province is to vary, is to increase in proportion to the increase of population or is to decrease if the population has decreased. That was the construction put upon this section of the British North America Act as far back as 1891, when, I think, Sir John Thompson, then Minister of Justice, decided in connection with the Representation Act at that time that the representation of Prince Edward Island should be reduced from six to five. So clear did it appear to all those who were in the House at that time, that this conclusion which was arrived at under the direction of Sir John Thompson was the correct one, that the point was never raised. Now, furthermore, when the question came up here recently and we considered it in connection with this readjustment, Prince Edward Island suggested that the matter should be referred to the Supreme Court for a formal decision. The matter was referred to the Supreme Court by the consent of both parties. The reference took place under section 37 of the Supreme Court Act, and upon that reference it was decided that the precedent established in 1891 was the correct one, and that in effect Prince Edward Island was to be treated like any other province, and that the representation had to be reduced to the number of members that is provided for in this Bill, that is to say, four. I heard it suggested by an hon. gentleman who represents one of the divisions of Prince Edward Island-I have forgotten which-that the judgment is not binding, and that this was the declaration of the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court. I would like to say to my hon. friend, who, perhaps has not had much experience in the Supreme Court, that the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court has simply followed the precedent which he established himself as far back as the Manitoba crossing case when he took it upon himself to declare that the opinion of the Supreme Court was not binding on any one. That is the personal opinion of the Chief Justice. It is not the opinion of the court and never was. As far as that court is concerned, I would like to declare in my capacity as Minister of Justice, that the Supreme Court was created by an Act of this parliament, and that therefore the Supreme Court is subject to the jurisdiction of this parliament, and if parliament decides to do anything in the direction

of fixing the jurisdiction of the work it is not) intended that it shall take upon itself to say that parliament has not the authority to do it. The Supreme Court exists, and has its being by virtue of our permission. We created the court, we have said that the court has a certain jurisdiction to exercise, or a certain function to perform and parliament is supreme in the matter. I want to say in so far as the Supreme Court is concerned, in justice to the other judges, that this is the opinion of the Chief Justice alone. It is not an opinion expressed for the first time now. It has been expressed before in the case that I have referred to. In my opinion the position taken by Sir John Thompson is the correct one. I agree absolutely with the finding of the Supreme Court; that is to say, that under existing conditions Prince Edward Island is entitled to four members. And, I have to go one step further and say that not only is it entitled to four members, but it is not in the power of this parliament to grant any more than it would be in the power of parliament to grant the province of Quebec any more than the number of members which is fixed by the British North America Act without reconsidering the whole question of representation as to all the provinces.

Mr. Speaker, I would not even presume to offer an opinion upon the point of order which has been raised in regard to which you, with all your experience and legal ability, have found so much doubt existing as to deter you from giving a ruling. But, I would offer a suggestion to the House. It appears to me that it would be very inconsistent, if not ridiculous to vote on a motion, which, if it were carried, would not be effective. I think we all feel that a motion of this kind would be unconstitutional. For that reason I think we might feel ourselves constrained to vote that this motion is not in order, and not a matter that can be dealt with in the manner in which it has been brought before the House at the present time.
speakername: The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS (Hon. James Sutherland).

speechtext: My hon. friend from West Prince, P.E.I. (Mr. Hackett) said that the province was going to appeal. Is that possible ? I am only asking for information. The explanation which the hon. Minister of Justice has given seems to be quite right. Could there be an appeal ?

The judgment of the Supreme Court is final in so far as it is in the power of this parliament to make a judgment of a Dominion court final, but we cannot overlook the fact that in the exercise of its prerogative the Privy Council has always the right, so far as the Privy Council advises His Majesty to authorize any subject or any province to appeal, and on a case being presented to the Privy Council they might allow an appeal, but that could only be done as a matter of grace. So far as our statute is concerned, this appeal is final, but on application being made to the Privy Council in England they may grant permission to appeal to His Majesty, and no such application has been made nor has such permission been granted.

Suppose the Privy Council gave the province of Prince Edward Island leave to appeal, heard its case and the decision of the Privy Council should be in accord with the claim presented by Prince Edward Island?
The effect would be that it would be our duty to amend the Act. That undoubtedly would be our duty. Of course, the Privy Council is absolutely supreme.

It seems to me that one difficulty we would be under in the case put by the Minister of Justice would be that an action in obedience to the Supreme Court to the Privy Council in England ; that appeal might not be considered for one or two years, and in the meantime this House, acting in obedience to the Supreme Court of Canada, might provide for the election of four members from the province of Prince Edward Island, and then, later on, we would find by the final decision of the courts that we had been all wrong and that Prince Edward Island was entitled to six members, so that during that time this House would be improperly constituted. The matter, I think, is one of very serious moment. I do not for a moment presume to dispute the legal proposition put forward by the hon. Minister of Justice, but I can see the very grave difficulties which might arise if we should, acting on the opinion of the Supreme Court of Canada, elect members from the different provinces! by reason of that opiniou,. and later on find, by the decision of the Privy Council in England that everything was wrong, that several provinces had been given representation to which they were not entitled, and that some had not received that representation to which they were entitled. I do not know into what state of confusion the legislation of this country would get under such circumstances. The Minister of Justice tells us, and no doubt correctly, that this House is after all the supreme tribunal of Cauada. Then I would ask the Minister of Justice what position we will be in, if we, the supreme tribunal, having ascertained the opinion of the Supreme Court, take action and then, upon obtaining a final opinion from the Privy Council, find that the Supreme Court is wrong ? We cannot consider the decision of that court conclusive under the circumstances put forward by the hon. member from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Hackett). It seems to be conceded, as a matter of fact, that that decision is not final, it is now under appeal and we are asked to deal with the question

in the House to-day as if it had been finally settled.

My hon. friend (Mr. Barker) must bear in mind that there is no appeal, there is not even an application, for leave to appeal, and in so far as this House is informed, there may never be an application for leave to appeal. Are we to suspend action for a year or two years in respect to this matter pending the decision of Prince Edward Island as to whether they shall appeal or not 1

That is one of the difficulties of the position which I am suggesting. The Minister of Justice tells us that no matter what any court in Canada may decide, this parliament is a supreme tribunal. Now, supposing that this supreme tribunal happens to differ even from the Supreme Court of Canada, where are we? Are we, sitting here as the supreme tribunal, to say that we must be governed by the decision of the Supreme Court in Canada whether we think it right or wrong ? The Minister of Justice tells us that there is no appeal. Well, there is certainly a right to appeal, and we are informed by the members from Prince Edward Island that an appeal has been applied for. Now, I can understand that we might find ourselves in-very grave difficulty if the Bill goes on, and we lay down a system of representation for the next ten years that under our constitution may turn out to be positively wrong. I suppose that what wre decide here now will govern absolutely for the next ten years, simply because, as the Minister of Justice says, this parliament is the supreme tribunal. We may act upon our judgment here and settle that Prince Edward Island is entitled to four members only, but we may find by the decision of the Privy Council in England that we are wrong, and that the representation of Prince Edward Island should be six, and then having settled our representation for Prince Edward Island for ten years, we would have to continue for the balance of that ten years if we acknowledge that we were in error. I submit that question as a subject for the consideration of the minister and one which shows that this matter should not be hastily decided. It has been brought up here as a question of order, and I think it requires a little more consideration that we are able to give it on the spur of the moment. Mr. Speaker hesitates to decide this question himself and to rule upon the question of order, and yet the House is asked on a moment's notice to decide upon this question of order, to go on with this measure and to settle for ten years what shall be the representation of that province. I am not undertaking to express an opinion as to whether our view is the right one, I am only endeavouring to show that the question is a very serious one, involving difficulties in any aspect of the case. And I Mr. BARKER.
do think this requires a little more consideration than it is possible for us to give it on the spur of the moment, especially Having regard to the fact that the hon. the Speaker hesitates to decide the point.
The' MINISTER OF JUSTICE. It does seem to me that it would be proper to suggest what the remedy is. What consideration can we give that will enable us to remedy these difficulties. My hon. friend (Mr. Barker) misunderstood wbat I said in respect to our power and our authority. Our power and authority over the Supreme Court of Canada is absolute, but it would not be so in case we undertook to put a certain construction on the British North America Act. Far from it; the British North America Act governs this parliament, and this parliament does not govern the British North America Act. We cannot touch, amend or in any way interfere with it. But so far as this particular question is concerned, provision is made for a reference of such constitutional questions to the Supreme Court. The parliament of Canada has said, by section 71 of the Supreme Court Act, that
The judgment of the Supreme Court shall in all cases be final and conclusive and no appeal shall be brought from any judgment or order of the Supreme Court to any court of appeal established by the parliament of Great Britain and Ireland by which appeals or petitions to Her Majesty in Council may be ordered to be heard.
So that so far as we are concerned this parliament has decided that the judgment of the Supreme Court is final and conclusive. But, of course, the right of appeal to His Majesty In Council, which is the right of every British subject, must necessarily continue to exist. We have declared that the judgment of the Supreme Court in such cases shall be final and conclusive, but we cannot take away from any British subject the right to go to the foot of the Throne and appeal to His Majesty. That is a right that may be exercised by the province of Prince Edward Island just as it may be by any private individual. But let me direct my hon. friend's attention to the fact that this appeal was disposed of in May last, and there was nothing to prevent the province of Prince Edward Island from petitioning His Majesty at either of the sittings of the Privy Council in June, July or August last. They have not chosen to do so.
How long have they a right to go there ?

That is a matter that is discretionary with the Privy Council. The lawyers were under the impression that the limit had been settled at six months. That was our view in the province of Quebec; but last summer the Privy Council decided to hear a petition for an appeal eleven mouths after judgment had been rendered. Therefore, although the

extreme limit Tip to the present has been a year, at the same time it is absolutely discretionary with His Majesty to listen to any grievance that any one of his subjects may have, and to grant leave to appeal at any time. We may fix by practice the limit of the time within which the petition for an appeal may be made; but undoubtedly the paramount right of His Majesty to hear a petition for an appeal exists at any time. If after the decision of the Supreme Court we were to stay our hand until in the dim and distant future it pleased those gentlemen to go to the Privy Council, where would it lead us to ? How could we legislate at all ?

Does the hon. Minister of Justice make any difference between a reference to the Supreme Court for an opinion and a suit between a province and the Dominion which is carried on appeal to the Supreme Court ?
In what way ?

It seems to me that the Act provides that the government may have reference to the Supreme Court at any time for its opinion in regard to the constitutionality of any measure before this House, by stating a case; and from my remembrance of the discussions in this House, it was stated by Mr. Blake, Mr. Mills and others, that the opinion of the Supreme Court under such circumstances would be hardly regarded as a judgment of the court, as it would in the case of an appeal carried to the Supreme Court in a suit between a province and the Dominion.
But the Supreme Court, having on the reference, decided that Prince Edward Island was in the same position as many other provinces-that it was only entitled to representation in proportion to its population -what are we to do about it ? If we did otherwise, what an injustice it would be to the other provinces. How could we justify our action towards Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Ontario, if we treated Prince Edward Island in that respect differently from the other provinces ?

Might I ask the hon. minister, do not the people of Prince Edward Island contend that there was some specific agreement made with them at the time they entered confederation as to the representation they should have in the House V

The people of Prince Edward Island contend that there was some private bargain or agreement between Prince Edward Island and the imperial authorities. But, so far as the Dominion of Canada is concerned, we are not bound by the negotiations; we are bound by the agreement which was actually made. Just as two private individuals may get together and make a bargain, and one may think that certain things were promised; but when you come to determine the contents of the agreement, you take the written instrument; so we are face to face with the British North America Act, so far as Prince Edward Island is concerned, in which we find that:
The population of Prince Edward Island having been increased by 15,000 and upwards since the year 1861, the island shall be represented in the House of Commons by six members.

There are two different classes of references provided for. There is the reference by the Governor in Council of any matter which they may think fit to refer, and the court shall thereupon hear and consider the same, and certify their opinion thereon to the Governor in Council. In addition to that, this parliament may refer any private Bill that comes up for consideration to two judges of the Supreme Court for their opinion. These are two different references altogether. In a matter of this sort, we might have gone on and legislated without reference to Prince Edward Island at all ; but as Prince Edward Island expressed a doubt with respect to our right to legislate in the direction in which we intended to legislate, and asked that the matter should be referred to the Supreme Court for the purpose of having that question set at rest, we conformed to their wish in that respect, though there was no obligation upon us to do so. If we could constitutionally give to Prince Edward Island what they contended for, five or six members, we would have been glad to do so; and we were solicitous to have the Supreme Court decide in that way if they could do so under the law.
Then it goes on to say :
The representation shall be readjusted from time to time under the provisions of the British North America Act.
The whole of this controversy turns on the meaning of the word ' readjustment.'

Might I call the attention of the Minister of Justice to the fact that when Prince Edward Island came in she had 95,857 inhabitants, which would entitle her to only five representatives in the Dominion House. Then, why was she given six ? Because she came in under special terms, and she stayed out from 1867 to 1873, until she got those special terms.

The answer is to be found in the paragraph which I have just read-that she got more than she was entitled to because her population had increased by 15,000 and upwards since the year 1861. But then it is provided that the representation is to be readjusted. What is the meaning of the word 'readjusted ' with respect to representation ?
That is what I would like to hear the minister say.

I think it would be useless for me to take up the time of the House discussing this matter further. I have stated the case from my standpoint, and all I can say is that my construction is the construction which was put on this Act in 1891 by the then Minister of Justice, and that that construction has since been confirmed by the Supreme Court of Canada; and nothing I could say could add any weight to what has already been done.

I think the hon. Minister of Justice has not answered the question which was put by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule). That hon. member pointed out that there were two kinds of cases which could be submitted to the Supreme Court-one in which their advice or opinion is sought in reference to a matter about which we have doubts as to the jurisdiction of this parliament. The hon. member for East Grey asked whether in that case there is an appeal to the Privy Council.
I am advised that there is not. That is my opinion.

That is my opinion also. We passed an Act of parliament for the purpose of obtaining the opinion of the Supreme Court in order to guide us in our deliberations. Whether we submitted to the court a stated case or whether we came before it as a litigant, I am not in a position to say, as I do not remember the facts.
We agreed with Prince Edward Island upon a case for reference.

In a case of that kind, I suppose that the Privy Council can exercise its appellate jurisdiction notwithstanding our statutory declaration in this measure that Prince Edward Island shall have four members. We cannot, by any legislation, interfere with the right of appeal or the prerogatives of the Crown. Let me put this case. The island was given six members upon entering confederation, and at the next decennial census its proportion of population to that of the province of Quebec had not changed. Is its representation to be diminished because, although it was given six members at confederation, it was not entitled to that many according to its population ?

I think that the Minister of Justice probably misapprehended the point I was trying to make. I was pointing to the difficulty that might arise from this question being decided as a point of order. The hon. gentleman says truly enough that we are acting under a written constitution and cannot depart from it. No doubt about that. Under certain clauses of an Act passed by this parliament, we have power Mr. HACKETT.
to take the opinion of the Supreme Court of Canada ; but although we get that opinion for our guidance, we are the final tribunal to decide the question. If we ask a judgment of the Supreme Court, that judgment, I presume, may be appealed from to the highest judicial tribunal in the empire, and I ask the Minister of Justice to consider this point. Supposing either the difficulties he suggests or those I suggest should arise, and we bring the question before parliament, and Mr. Speaker, in his discretion, decides, as a point of order, that they can not be discussed, surely that would be a very dangerous position to take. Would it not be dangerous to argue that our right to discuss a question after the Supreme Court has given its opinion upon a particular point relating to the constitution, is to be shut off on the decision of Mr. Speaker ?
I did not argue that.

That is the question raised on the point of order. I submit that it is not properly speaking a point of order at all. Admitting all the objections raised by the Minister of Justice, and all the difficulties that may arise from our deciding wrongly, surely the question whether those difficulties are to be met with in some particular way or not, is a question, not for Mr. Speaker to decide as a point of order, but for the House to discuss and consider ? We might discuss and give full weight to the question of the necessity of waiting for a decision from the supreme judicial tribunal. Supposing the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada had been that Prince Edward Island was entitled to six members, and that the government of Canada, believing that decision to be wrong had immediately appealed to the Privy Council in England, and that in the meantime Mr. Speaker were to rule that the Supreme Court, having decided that six was- a proper representation from Prince Edward Island, any proposition to give it four members only was out of order, surely all the difficulties I have spoken of would arise ? It may be that they will arise in any case, but it does seem to me that it is not a question upon which Mr. Speaker should prevent discussion. We might, as parliament, discuss whether it was wise or opportune to act according to or against the opinion of the Supreme Court of Canada under the circumstances. We might come to the conclusion that it was extremely dangerous to set at naught its opinions, and to say that there shall be only four representatives, when the Supreme Court decided that the province was entitled to six, but surely that is a question for us to consider and not for Mr. Speaker to decide. It is not a point of order at all, but a question to be submitted to parliament, and when it comes before parliament for discussion, it is proper for the Minister of Justice to place before par-

liament the difficulties, dangers and troubles that might arise from a mistaken action on the part of the government. But it is not a question for Mr. Speaker to decide offhand, and say that we shall be precluded from considering those difficulties.

I do not understand your decision, Mr. Speaker, to be that which my hon. friend has explained. I understand the effect of your decision to be that, in view of the doubt which has been raised and which you say you entertain, you will not take the responsibility of ruling this motion out of order. That I understand, Sir, to be your decision. You have not ruled that because the Supreme Court has given a certain opinion, therefore the motion is out of order. You have mentioned that as an incident in the question submitted to you, but you have said that you will not take the responsibility of ruling that the amendment is out of order. On the question itself, if any word or act of mine would help my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island to secure two additional members for that province he would have my vote and sympathy.
I shall propose a method by which the hon. minister can help us out.

If by any act or word of mine I could give Prince Edward Island two more members, I would do so most cheerfully. If by any act or word of mine I could prevent the reduction of members in Nova Scotia I would do it most cheerfully. I would with equal alacrity do the same thing for New Brunswick. I will go further, and say that if I could prevent the reduction in the province of Ontario by any act of mine, I would be glad to 'do it. It is to be regretted that in the foundation of the confederation some arrangement was not made which would have prevented the reduction of representation in these provinces and have made allowance for a fair and equitable redistribution by adding to the members of the other provinces without diminishing those of the smaller provinces, which are particularly interested, though the principle would apply to Ontario as well. In Prince Edward Island, a small province, they look upon this matter with great interest and a certain degree of jealousy. They had originally six members and were reduced to five, and now they are reduced to four. It is not surprising that members from Prince Edward Island, and the citizens of that province should view this with anxiety and desire, if possible, to avoid this reduction. But, under the advice of our Minister of Justice and other eminent lawyers who have been consulted, the government came to the conclusion that it had to be. The question was referred to the Supreme Court and their unanimous judgment given ; and so long
as that judgment remains I think we are bound to respect it. If my hon. friend can move that Prince Edward Island be allowed two members, my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) can move that Ontario be allowed her six, and I that Nova Scotia be allowed her two. If the matter is open to the mere vote of the majority of this House, we will all arrange it very happily. But the best information we have is that as a matter of law and as a matter of the constitution we cannot give these six members to Prince Edward Island ; and, that being the case I do hope that hon. gentlemen will see that there is no disposition to be ungenerous to the Island, but that those of us who differ from him differ only because it seems to us that the law makes it necessary. I do not consider that the case of Ontario, Quebec or any other province is the same as that of Prince Edward Island. The members from Prince Edward Island are not coming here as beggars asking this House to grant two more members, but they support this motion because they say Prince Edward Island is entitled to six members under the terms of confederation and under the terms of the British North America Act. We know the terms of confederation, and we know that from 1867 to 1873, Prince Edward Island stood out of the union for the express reason that at every conference she had stipulated that, owing to her peculiar isolated position, she should have six members in this House oif Commons. I went fully into that point when I spoke on this question before, I do not think that any hon. member on the other side of the House will dispute that the intention of the representatives of Prince Edward Island at this conference was to stipulate that six representatives should be given in perpetuity for Prince Edward Island. The question of law came up, and the hon. Minister of Justice stated that he did not agree with the representations made by the legislature of Prince Edward Island to the effect that that province was entitled to six members in perpetuity. Therefore the question was submitted on reference to the Supreme Court. The question was submitted under authority of the Supreme and Exchequer Court Acts as amended by the Act 54-5 Vic., chap-terter 25, to amend the Act 335 of the Revised Statutes, intituled an Act respecting the Supreme and Exchequer Courts. The question submitted was the following :
Although the population of Prince Edward Island, as ascertained in the census ot 1901, if divided by the unit of representaion ascertained by dividing the number of 65 Into the population of Quebec is not sufficient to give six members in the House of Commons of Canada to that province, is the representation of Prince Edward Island in the House of Commons of Canada, liable under the British North America Act,

1867, and amendments thereto and the terms of union of 1873 under which that province entered confederation, to ibe reduced below six the number granted to that province by the said terms of union of 1873.
That was the question to he decided. And as the lion. Minister of Justice has said, the chief justice and his associate judges decided that Prince Edward Island was not entitled to six members. But, at the same time, the chief justice said it was only an opinion, that this was not an ordinary case, and they would not give a judgment, and so it was not binding ou anybody. Now I understand that the Prince Edward Island legislature was to make an appeal to the Privy Council, and as I believe the Prime Minister said in his remarks the other night that it was certain that this appeal would be taken. In that case, the point of tire hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) was well taken. There is, apparently, a grave doubt as to the interpretation of the Act of Confederation of 1873, whether Prince Edward Island is entitled to six members. It seems unfair that, while an appeal to the Privy Council is pending, she should be reduced to four members, when this appeal may take years to decide. It seems to me that'the remedy lies in the hands of the government, to allow Prince Edward Island six members and let the appeal go on. I may say that the clause under which Prince Edward Island was allowed six members is as follows :
That the population of Prince Edward Island having been Increased by 15,000 or upwards since the year 1861, the island should he represented in the House of Commons of Canada by six members.
Now, it appears to me that the representatives of Prince Edward Island and the Dominion made that stipulation knowing that the population of the Island amounted at that time to 95.857. They were not taking into consideration the unit of representation as found by dividing 65 into the population of Quebec, but they intended evidently that they were stipulating that Prince Edward Island should have six members in perpetuity because of her isolated position, and because of her peculiar circumstances. The delegates realized and pointed out that they did not expect that Prince Edward Island would keep pace with the other provinces and that if she would give up her right to self government, she wanted some rights guaranteed to her in this House. And it seems to me that the balance of the clause,
-the representation to be readjusted from time to time under the provisions of the British North America Act.
-can only refer to the case of her population increasing, and intended to provide that, if she was entitled to more than six members by reason of increase of population, the addition to her representation should be made, hut that no deduction was to he made Sir. LEFURGEY.
by reason of the population of Quebec increasing more rapidly than the population of Prince Edward Island. Now, to strengthen this case I would refer to the case of British Columbia. That province came in under the same terms as Prince Edward Island, except that, 'readjustment' was used in one case and ' increase' in the other. But in the case of British Columbia it has been held that the intention of the parties in agreeing to confederation must be considered. We find that in 1892 the right hon. leader of the present government said :
But at the same time I am myself taken by surprise at the objection raised-
Referring to an objection raised to British Columbia retaining six members.
-for it has always been underitood that British Columbia was entitled to six members.
Again he said :
We hove always understood that British Columbia was entitled to six memibens until such time that she was entitled to a larger number, but that she should not be represented by a less number than six. Fur my part I would be sorry to come to any conclusion which would deprive British Columbia of that which the people suppose themselves to be their right.
This case was not taken to the Supreme Court although there was a grave doubt in the minds of the lawyers in this House as to whether British Columbia was entitled to six members. This House decided the matter. The present leader of the government said that it was a matter of intention, that British Columbia was entitled to six members and that he would be sorry to take away the rights that the people thought they had at confederation. I say that this is the same position as Prince Edward Island is in at the present time, and the same rule the right hou. gentleman then laid down as applying to British Columbia should now be applied to Prince Edward Island. We are certainly going to be in an anomalous position in Prince Edward Island, if our representation is to be lowered after every decennial census. We started out with six. We are to have four under this readjustment. In ten years we may have only three. Then would appear this anomaly-we shall still have four Senators representing us in tiie Upper House while there will be only three members from Prince Edward Island in this House. It certainly was never intended that we should have fewer members than six. The confederation documents themselves show that this House has no right to take away from the representation of Prince Edward Island as It was when she first entered confederation. Now, the chief justice of the Supreme Court himself said that the intention of the parties might he used in interpreting this Act, and that the intention might he gathered from the circumstances attending the entrance of this province to confederation. And I contend that the circumstances in connection witlr

tlie island, and the conferences that were had, and the dehates at that time, and the wording of the clause giving her representation of six members, amply justify this parliament in giving expression to the manifest intention of the parties and retaining these six members for Prince Edward Island. This is the court, in conjunction with the imperial authorities, that gave us these rights, and this is the court that should interpret the intention of the parties to confederation. Now the representatives here of Prince Edward-Island and the legislature of Prince Edward Island are contending that by the Act of Confederation, and' by the expressed intention of the confederation documents, together with extraneous evidence, we are entitled to six members, and we ask that before the appeal is had to the Privy Council, and until the same is decided, the six members be left to Prince Edward Island. Should it be afterwards' decided that a more equitable adjustment of the terms of confederation might be had with regard to that province, the matter can be dealt with at that time. But to take away our representatives now to which we think we are justly entitled, seems to be taking an unfair advantage of us. The chief justice said at that time,-in answer to a question :
Could readjustment mean anything different for Prince Edward Island than It does for the rest of the Dominion.
lit might, my Lord, but I am not baking that branch of the argument.

It might be that it was the impression of Prince Edward Island at the tame, In the minds of the public men when they consented to this, that they did not expect a decrease, but that is not a consideration in the interpretation of a clear Act of parliament.
Now I make this appeal to the government, that justice he given Prince Edward Island, and that she he left with six members until the matter can be brought before the Privy Council, or nntil equitable adjustment be secured by an address from this parliament and the provincial legislature to the Imperial authorities. The manifest intention of the parties to confederation was that justice should he given to Prince Edward Island. It was recommended by the imperial authorities that justice be given to Prince Edward Island. Now, I would suggest to the Finance Minister and his colleagues that an address be sent from this House and from the provincial House to the imperial authorities, giving expression to the real intention of the parties to confederation, which evidently was that we should have six representatives in this House. I would suggest to the Minister of Justice that that course he taken, which was suggested to me by the leader of the House at six o'clock. I would like to have the opinion of the Minister of Justice on the question.

,T. EOGAN (Cumberland). The proposition to present an address to His 390
Majesty to amend the British North America Act, I think is well worthy of the consideration of parliament, and particularly to those of us who are living in the provinces which are being bereft of members. But what has that to do with the Bill now before the House ? That is another matter entirely. If we are going to present an address to the imperial authorities to amend the British North America Act, let us take it up in a proper time and place. We cannot present such an address at the present time. No one can help but regret that a province situated as Prince Edward Island is should have to lose another member after It has already lost one member following the previous decennial census. I suppose it was for that reason, among others, that it was agreed by the government to refer this matter to the highest court we have in Canada for its opinion. Let me draw attention to the fact that the Supreme Court, with absolute unanimity, rendered a decision that the province is only entitled to four members. Now the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) said : Supposing we only allow four members to Prince Edward Island, and afterwards the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council should decide that it was entitled to six members, then vve would be in a very anomalous position. Let me point out to him how much more anomalous our position would be if, in spite of the fact that we have the judgment of the highest court of our land, in spite of the fact that we have the opinion of Sir John Thompson and of the present able and' distinguished Minister of Justice, if in spite of these things to the contrary, we now proceeded to give Prince Edward Island six members instead of four, and supposing that a dissolution of this parliament should take place and six. members were returned from Prince Edward Island, we would have an unconstitutional parliament in this country ; and I point out to the member for Hamilton that the consequences of that condition of affairs would be much more serious than the consequences that were pointed out by him, for we would he doing it in face of the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada, which is the highest authority we have.
Mr, BARKER. Would not parliament he equally unconstitutional whether it has too many or too few ?

Suppose you admit that parliament would be equally unconstitutional by having too many as by having too few; hut if we only have four members from Prince Edward Island, we are carrying out the instructions of the highest court of interpretation of the British North America Act that we have. Now is it reasonable that we should fly in face of the Supreme Court of Canada, interpreting, not a Dominion Statute hut an Imperial Statute ? Should we fly in the face of the most distinguished jurists in Canada in the in-



terpretation tliey put upon the British North America Act, as we would be doing if we granted the request of Prince Edward Island ? I think It would be in the best Interests of the province of Prince Edward Island, in fact it is the only position for us to take, now to reduce the representation to four members, much as we regret it. As I say, it is a matter of serious consideration to us of the older provinces, and at a proper time I think we should consider the presentation of an address to His Majesty praying for an amendment to the British North America Act respecting the representation of the provinces of the Dominion of Canada.

,T. HUGHES (King's, P.E.I.). I want to say a word or two on this question. We all very much regret, and the people of Prince Edward Island very much regret, that their delegates to the confederation conference overlooked the probability of a great growth in the population of Quebec, and therefore failed to provide for the representation of Prince Edward Island being left for all time to come at six members. There is no doubt in the minds of our people that that was an oversight on the part of our delegates. A provision like that might possibly and would probably have been obtained at the time we entered confederation. We also regret that this matter was not more fully gone into in 1891, when our representation was first reduced. But we must abide by the constitution under which we live. I was going to suggest to my hon, friend from Prince County (Mr. Hackett) whether we should! not be very careful here to do nothing that might prejudice our case in any way when it comes to be taken up before the Privy Council. Of course I am not a lawyer, and I may make a. mistake in what I am going to say now ; but as I listened to the Minister of Justice to-night I heard him say that this parliament was the highest court in the land, and that if this matter was pressed to a decision here to-night, this House in all probability would have to vote to uphold the constitution according to the interpretation given by the Supreme Court.
Now, would a vote given by this House along those lines prejudicially affect our case in any way when it was taken before the Privy Council ? If it would have that effect, I would ask the hon. member for West Prince, who has moved this amendment to carefully consider whether it would not be in the best interests of Prince Edward Island to withdraw his amendment. An adverse vote of this House would be an important matter. If a vote given by this House would prejudicially affect our case when it is brought before the Privy Council, would it not be worth the while of the hon. gentleman to take into consideration whether or not it would not be better to withdraw his amendment. That is the point Mr. LOGAN.
I wish to make. If my hon. friend (Mr. Gilmour) had sat on this committee for about three and a half months, had considered all these matters in the committee and had them discussed for weeks in this House I think he would come to the conclusion either that he had no mind to make up or that it was time to come to some conclusion as to what

should be done. As a member of the committee, I am perfectly satisfied, and I am satisfied to leave it to the people of Toronto. Toronto js a strongly Conservative city, but its inhabitants are people of intelligence. My hon. friend from Centre Toronto referred to the fact that Toronto is sometimes spoken of as Hog-town.
You do not believe that.

I do not believe that ; I do not like the name. But I can understand why, if such pretentions are put forward by the member for Centre Toronto, we sometimes hear that name applied to them. It is inevitable under all the conditions that as my hon. friend from Middlesex says, there must be anomalies. Any one must see that anomalies must result from the adoption of the principle of county boundaries. For instance, Prince Edward county in Ontario, has a population of some 18,000, and Lincoln has over 30,000, but these differences must occur. We must remember that Ontario is losing six members from its previous representation, and when this committee came to consider the representation of Ontario, I think they dealt liberally with the city of Toronto, and I must say, with some feeling, that the words used in reference to the action of the committee on this Bill have been as to some great injustice being done to the city of Toronto are most unwarranted. There is not the slightest foundation for such a statement, and I leave it to the people of the country, to the people residing in the rural constituencies, and to the members of this House, to decide if Toronto has not been fairly treated. In the past large commercial centres have been dealt with arbitrarily, and that is not unfair in view of the fact that they have a larger representation in the House in other ways and have opportunities of influencing the opinions of this House that other municipalities have not, and I say that we dealt most liberally and generously with the city of Toronto. There might have been cause for grumbling if we had not given Toronto an extra member, but taking everything into consideration, I think it is a disingenuous argument to say that because the unit of Toronto is
41,000,	and in some other county it is less, an injustice has been done. You have to consider the whole province, and I am willing to leave it to the people of Toronto'to decide as to the fairness of the action of the committee. We could not have come to a better conclusion in the interest of Toronto without dealing most unjustly and unfairly with the balance of the province. Several gentlemen from Toronto made wild and extravagant statements as to the injustice done to Toronto, and I expected that we would hear some evidence and arguments to bear out these extravagant statements, but I am satisfied now that I was right,in my first conclusion, and that they
have no foundation for their wild statements. That city has been fairly treated and no amendment has been moved by the opposition members as to the division which has been fairly made, without regard to party politics, and I repeat that I am quite *satisfied to leave this matter to the people of Toronto and of Ontario.
