I desire to make a very few remarks in connection with this redistribution so far as it affects the province of Manitoba, and to ip-troduce an amendment to the Bill in that regard. I shall try to do so without the vehemence of expression or without quite so much desk-pounding as the last speaker gave us an exhibition of, Sir Knight, though he be. The debate was going on in a calm and business-like manner until that hon. gentleman got up. Yet, after speaking for half an hour, taking up the time of the House, obstructing the progress of this government measure, he sat down without having said a single word in defence of the redistribution that has been made so far as the city of Toronto is concerned. It is amusing to hear the hon. gentleman lecturing the House about sincerity-this hon. gentleman who moved a resolution in this House under which, if it had come into effect, it would have been a misdemeanour for the government to appoint any hon. member for this House to a position of emolument under the Crown, yet who has sat here as a member of a government that has appointed upwards of a score of members to office.
The objection I have to the redistribution in the province of Manitoba is largely because of the departure that is made from the principle laid down by the Prime Minister when he introduced the measure into this House. As this has been so thoroughly discussed in the committee stage, I shall content myself with moving my amendment, and giving a very few reasons why that amendment should be carried. The first plan submitted by the Liberals in regard to the redistribution of the province of Manitoba, as I stated the other day, provided for the division of the boundaries of no less than eleven municipalities. This, of course, was in direct violation of the principle laid down by the Prime Minister. And, while several of the changes as proposed in the Conservative proposition, have been acquiesced in it is because of the fact that we maintained municipal boundaries.

Now, this Bill as.it remains at the present time, will divide no less than five municipalities. In one constituency alone, the constituency of Dauphin, they divided no less than three municipalities, Rosedale, Lans-downe and Westbourne There is no possible justification for the division of those municipalities, and it is largely because of that division that there were two plans submitted to the committee. They also took in the municipality of Posen east of Lake Manitoba, the municipality of Posen, which has no community of interest whatever with the other portion of the division. Now, in the constituency of Portage la Prairie they are dividing the municipality of Portage la Prairie; I do not know why they did that. The municipality of Portage la Prairie is included in the constituency of that name for the local riding, and they might well have followed the same boundary. This was the main point of difference between the two plans submitted by the respective parties before that committee. Had they included the municipality of Portage la Prairie entirely without dividing it, they would have come very ciose to the plan that was submitted by the Conservative members. Now, in the constituency of Macdonald they have divided but one municipality, Rosser, making in all five municipalities that they have divided under the operation of this Bill. Now, Mr. Speaker, because of those municipal divisions, and also because their population is not nearly so equal as it would have been under the proposition submitted by the Conservatives, I beg to move this amendment, which contains the substance of the amendments that were moved by the leader of the opposition and were voted down by the Liberal members of the committee :

Therefore, I was under the impression that there had been some arrangement arrived at. I suppose the hon. Postmaster General would agree that there is no object from the standpoint of either party that we should stand up twelve or fifteen times to-night to record our votes when we have recorded them in the first place. I also desire to offer an amendment and as I have already spoken in regard to the question no good purpose would be served by making any extended remarks because I have already gone over the matter. This is an amendment in regard to the redistribution in Nova Scotia which was discussed by the hon. Minister of Finance (Horn. Mr. Fielding) by the members from Cape Breton and by myself when the matter came up in committee. The amendment is as follows :
That all the words after '. be ' to the end of the question be left out, and that the words ' recommitted to a Committee of the Whole House with instructions that they have power to so amend the same that the county of Cape Bre-tou shall return two members as at present.

I understood that my hon. friend intended to move the same motion as he proposedi on the previous occasion. The previous motion was that the counties of Richmond and Victoria be united and in this he has dealt with only one part of the question.

My recollection is not that I moved any motion, but that I suggested that the counties of Richmond and Victoria should be joined. One of my hon. friends from Cape Breton pointed out an alternative proposition of which I had never before heard, and I desire not to commit myself to any definite proposals beyond this, but it seems to me that whatever alternative is adopted Cape Breton should not be added to the county of Victoria and the united counties divided as at present.
I think that the report of the minority of the committee included a recommendation that the county of Victoria and Richmond should be united. That was the representation made by my hon. friend.
Yes, I did move it in the committee.

It was also discussed in the House and I understand that it was the motion which my hon.



friend was making. He now moves quite ' a different proposition which does not meet the difficulty because it does not tell us from what constituency a member is to be taken ; it is only a partial measure. It was admitted in discussion that one member should be taken from Cape Breton Island. If my hon. friend proposed to give Cape Breton two members and stated from what constituency he would take the other member, then this would be a matter for consideration. But he failed to do that, and the motion in its present form is absolutely ineffective.

Whatever criticism may be made from the point of view the Minister of Finance has pointed out I am willing to have attached to the motion.
I was of the opinion, and so moved in the committee, that Victoria and Richmond should be joined. Objections of a very decided character were made to that in the House and one hon. gentleman pointed out an alternative which I had not considered before and have not yet considered. I would regard either of these alternatives as preferable to uniting the two counties of Cape Breton and Victoria and dividing the united comity as js provided for in the Bill as it stands at present. And my motion is directed to the end that the county of Cape Breton shall return two members as at present and that one of the alternatives presented by myself and the hon. gentleman from Cape Breton should be adopted in place of the present division.

This motion will leave us with one more member from the province of Nova Scotia than the number which we have resolved that that province should have. You cannot eat your cake and have it and I wish to point out the fact that this leaves the province one more member than it is entitled to. I therefore could not undertake to support it.
The hon. leader of the opposition referred to a statement of the hon. chairman of the committee (Mr. Hyman) as being incorrect, and as doing him some injustice in regard to a number of divisions.
No.
Then I did not understand liis language.

I did not hear what my hon. friend said, and I stated that if there was any expression in his speech about unanimity in the committee differing from my statement in regard to this Bill then I would desire to reiterate the statements I had made when in Committee of the Whole, which I understood, were not controverted by hon, members opposite who were members of the committee. I do not know that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hyman) made any statement inconsistent with what Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
I had stated, but if he did I wish to say that what I said was well founded.

My hon. friend did not refer to the proceedings in the committee but to what took place when we were in Committee of the Whole House. There is no difference of opinion as to the ainendments which were moved in committee as they are on record.
I thought, from my hon. friend the action of my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) in the committee and the House, that he was not always well informed in regard to Ontario matters and I thought he would not have submitted one of the propositions which he made if he had known its objects and I repeat that I do not think that there is any warrant for the statement made as to to the political effect of this division, as to its being a gerrymander. I think I was perfectly fair and I am prepared to allow the two propositions to be compared by the people. I wish to point out that a great majority of these suggested divisions have not been moved in the House so that a comparison could be made by the country.

I can add nothing to what I said when the question was before the committee a few days ago. Two propositions which were considered by the committee having this in charge were before the House a few evenings ago. The proposition with regard to Cape Breton in the resolution which the leader of the opposition has now placed in your hands is an entirely different proposition from that enunciated here a few evenings ago, and which he and his associates on the committee presented in the committee. When this matter was up the other evening I said that I would support either one of the propositions. So far as the proposition made by the leader of the opposition to-night is concerned I would support it more strongly than I did the proposition submitted a few evenings ago. There is every reason why I should support the giving of two members to Cape Breton, but the constitution of the country demands that certain reductions shall be made in the representation of Nova Scotia, and so long ns I have a seat in this House I am prepared to observe what the constitution demands. I must recognize that the province of Nova Scotia as at present constituted is bound to lose two seats in the present redistribution. It was decided by a majority of the committee that the county of Victoria and the county of Cape Breton should be united for the purpose of representation.
A counter proposition was made by the minority to the effect that the county of Victoria and the county of Richmond should be united, and the county of Cape Breton left undisturbed. The proposition submitted to-night is an entirely different proposition, and it Is one which does not at all answer the purpose which the committee has in

view. If any proposition is to be submitted to this House, I think it only fair that something should be said as to what that proposition is. The simple proposition to leave the province of Nova Scotia as *t is at the present time I do not think can be entertained by this House. The present proposition is not a reasonable or a practicable one. However, I have nothing at all to add to what I said the other evening. Two practical propositions were then submitted to the House, and for my part, I consider that we had to choose between two evils. We had to recognize that something had to be done, and I was prepared to support the proposition that was submitted on that occasion ; but the present proposition is not a practicable one, and does not meet the requirements of the province of Nova Scotia.

If the hon. leader of the opposition is under the misapprehension that I said anything in the House to-day conveying the impression that any motion or action of his in the committee was inconsistent with his action in the House, I desire to remove that misapprehension from his mind. It may have arisen in this way, that in the amendment handed in by the hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) in one of the rules in regard to the unit, it was stated that the unit should be made by deducting from the total population the population of the city of Toronto; and I -simply pointed out that it was declared in the record that the population of all the cities should be deducted from the unit, and not the city of Toronto alone.

I do not think there is any question between us as to what took place in the committee. We moved first that all the cities of Ontario should have their representation fixed, and that the unit should be then fixed by dividing the balance of the population by the remaining number of members. That was mot accepted by the majority of the committee, and then the representation of the city of Toronto was arbitrarily fixed and the unit determined in that way. I remember that we registered a formal protest in the committee against confining the representation of Toronto to five members. I am sure there was no difference in regard to that. Now, the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Johnston) thinks this resolution is not practicable. I wish to point out to the hon. member that in the Bill itself eighteen members are assigned to the province of Nova Scotia. My resolution proposes that the committee shall have instructions to so amend the schedule that the county of Cape Breton shall retain two members. It is true, I did not add the proposition which I ma'de before the committee. I have already stated my reason for that, the reason being that another proposition which I had not previously heard of was made in the 391}
House, and I am not sure that it was not a better one than the one I submitted to the committee. But by proposing that the Bill should be so amended as to give the county of Cape Breton two members, I thought, and still think, I was giving the committee ample powers for the purpose I indicated.

The hon. leader of the opposition admits, however, that something had to be done, and that something had to be done in the Island of Cape Breton. There was a proposition made in the House by my hon. colleague, to join Victoria and Inverness. The other vras made by himself-to join- Victoria and Richmond. The proposition of the hon. leader of the opposition is one to join Victoria with Richmond or Inverness or to disfranchise it altogether.

I humbly submit that we cannot intelligently vote for a motion of this kind without asking what is the point with which it is connected. We know that the Island of Cape Breton, containing these four counties, which now has five members, will only have four. I submit that when the hon. member proposes that Cape Breton shall retain its two members and declines to make in his motion any -statement as to where the other member is to come from, it cannot commend itself to the sound judgment of any member of the House.

tanio, which it was to the advantage of these hon. gentlemen to gerrymander, that they did not gerrymander. True, they have since gone back on a part of their work. speechtext: I also urn very glad that this motion has been moved. But I am sorry .to hear the speech of the lion. Minister of Customs, as it is another illustration of his unfairness. That hon. gentleman has complained many times of the redistribution of 1882, yet he seeks to justify opposition to this amendment. He talks about representation by population and the principle laid down by the hon. member for South Norfolk. Why, when this Bill was introduced we were told that there were two principles maintained in it, one the maintenance of county boundaries and the other *the equalization of population as far as possible. Both these principles were violated. And that is what I complain of. The hon. Minister of Customs ridicules the idea of having Brantford, with a population of 16,019, as one constituency and the rural part of Brant county, with a population of 21,521, as another. The hon. gentleman knows perfectly well that Brantford's population is nearly 20,000 to-day, and growing fast. And he knows also that if you take the population of Brantford and also the Indians, who have no votes, and who number 3,771, the city of Brantford will have a greater population than the rural part of the couuty. Yet he is willing to place the disfranchised Indian against the intelligent elector of Brantford. If the hon. gentleman really wants to equalize the population he could put Brantford and Tuscarora together. But the whole Idea is to secure two Liberal members for the county of Brantford, including the city of Brantford. I would not object so much to this redistribution if hon. gentlemen opposite were to come out fairly and say they were going to make a redistribution to defeat the Conservative party. But what I dislike and detest is to see these hon. gentlemen roll their eyes heavenward ffnd thank God that they are not like these wicked Tories, but are going to give a fair distribution, when this redistribution is the very reverse bf fair. Personally, I have no favours to ask these hon. gentlemen; I am simply comparing their professions of fairness with their acts, as shown in this Bill. It is for the electors to decide whether this measure is fair or not. For my part, I am satisfied that we shall have no difficulty in showing the electors that this is a most unfair measure, and that the redistribution of the county of Brant is one of the worst instances of unfairness that it covers. this case, for the redistribution has to be made on the basis of the census. But I wish to say distinctly that I do not know that Brantford has a population of 20,000. FOWLER (King's, N.B.) The hon. Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) seemed to think it a great discrepancy to have a difference of 5,000 in the population of two constituencies. As between provinces.

AI >.TOURNMENT-ILL-TREATMENT OF TRAVELLERS AT NEWPORT, VT.

Mr. Speaker, before the House adjourns, I would tike to draw attention to a statement which appears in the Montreal ' Star ' tonight-and a similar statement appeared in the papers this morning-respecting the disgraceful treatment given to two gentlemen who were in attendance at the recent meeting of the Chambers of Commerce of the empire at Montreal. I will pass the paper over to the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding). The story told of the indignities heaped upon these gentlemen in crossing the border at Newport, Vermont, is certainly one that should be promptly and fully investigated by the government. I think representations should be made to the proper authorities in the United States, so that similar treatment will not be dealt out to any other gentlemen who are passing from this country to the United States on their way to take ship upon the voyage homeward. This is a most disgraceful episode. I will read what the report says :
Two distinguished members of the Chambers of Commerce of the empire were, on the 23rd instant, held up at Newport, V(t., a border town between the United States and Canada, at which is stationed a United States immigration officer.
The gentlemen in question are Mr. William Callard, representing the Torquay Board of Trade, and Mr. John Falconer, representing the Dover Board of Trade. These gentlemen came out to Canada via the St. Lawrence, some weeks ago, and, after making the tour of Canada, were on their way back to England via Boston.
They were not aware that, according to the United States immigration laws, they were subject to being held up, or they probably would have either proceeded back to England via the St. Lawrence, or have taken the precautions of applying to the United States immigration officers in Montreal, for the necessary certificate, which would ensure their not being inconvenienced while en route to Boston, there to do business and eventually sail for home.
The following letter, which is now in the hands of Mr. Arthur J. Hodgson, president of the board ,of trade, from the gentlemen in question, pretty fully explains the incident :
On station at Newport, September 23, 1903.
Mr. Falconer and I are hung up here, having been taken out of the train, not being in possession of a medical certificate. We booked from Windsor station, Montreal, to Boston, at 9 a.m. Our baggage passed inspection at Montreal and the hand baggage on the train. The immigration inspector made al] inquiries and took our age, position, name, and also inquired if we had any money, and then consulted his colleague, and both insisted we could not proceed, and took our hand baggage from the train and we had to follow.
Tile inspector then telephoned or telegraphed to Montreal, asking whether if we were to be returned to Montreal or allowed to go on to Boston. In about an hour we were informed we could proceed on our giving the number of our return steamship ticket.
We find we cannot leave for Boston until 11,35 to-night, and, therefore, shall not be in Boston until 7,30 to-morrow morning.

Kindly let those delegates who intend visiting the States know that they may be subject to the same outrage.
Yours faithfully.

Tlie ' Star ' report goes on to say that the receipt of this letter created a sensation among the business men of Montreal. I am sure that the authorities proper of the United States are not cognizant of any such treatment being meted out to gentlemen passing over to that country, and I think that the government ought to make some representations to prevent the possibility of a recurrence of such treatment. I shall take the liberty of sending the pa per over to the hon. Minister of Finance.

However much we may regret that these gentlemen have been subjected to any discourtesy I am by no means clear that we can do anything in the matter. If our American neighbours choose to pass laws which we think are unreasonable we have to acknowledge their right to do so. However, the hon. gentleman having drawn attention to the matter it will be looked into.
